claims.claim: TEDC1 and TEDC2 physically interact with TUBD1 and TUBE1.
claims.source: These proteins physically interact with TUBD1 and TUBE1 (Breslow et al., 2018; Huttlin et al., 2017; Huttlin et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Loss of Tedc1 or Tedc2 in 3T3 cells results in a variable distribution of centriole numbers through the cell cycle.
claims.source: Loss of Tedc1 or Tedc2 in 3T3 cells results in a variable distribution of centriole numbers through the cell cycle, and tagged TEDC1 localizes to centrosomes (Breslow et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Breslow et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Tagged TEDC1 localizes to centrosomes in 3T3 cells.
claims.source: Loss of Tedc1 or Tedc2 in 3T3 cells results in a variable distribution of centriole numbers through the cell cycle, and tagged TEDC1 localizes to centrosomes (Breslow et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Breslow et al., 2018.

claims.claim: TEDC1-/- and TEDC2-/- mutant cells were created in the same background as the TUBD1-/- and TUBE1-/- mutants (hTERT RPE-1 TP53-/-).
claims.source: We created TEDC1-/- or TEDC2-/- mutant cells in the same background as the TUBD1-/- and TUBE1-/- mutants and found that these cells phenocopy loss of TUBD1 or TUBE1.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the methods and data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: TEDC1-/- and TEDC2-/- cells phenocopy loss of TUBD1 or TUBE1.
claims.source: We created TEDC1-/- or TEDC2-/- mutant cells in the same background as the TUBD1-/- and TUBE1-/- mutants and found that these cells phenocopy loss of TUBD1 or TUBE1.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 1 showing similar phenotypes.

claims.claim: Compound microtubules are required for recruiting the helical inner scaffold.
claims.source: We find that the compound microtubules are required for recruiting the helical inner scaffold and correctly positioning the proximal end.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 4E showing absence of inner scaffold proteins in mutant centrioles.

claims.claim: Compound microtubules are required for correctly positioning the proximal end.
claims.source: We find that the compound microtubules are required for recruiting the helical inner scaffold and correctly positioning the proximal end.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 4F-I showing elongated proximal end in mutant centrioles.

claims.claim: Centrioles formed de novo are very similar to procentrioles formed by templated centriole duplication in composition and architecture.
claims.source: As part of our analysis, we also determine the composition and architecture of centrioles formed de novo and find that these are very similar to those of procentrioles formed by templated centriole duplication.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparative data in Figure 4 showing similar protein localization patterns.

claims.claim: Compound microtubules are required for scaffolding substructures within centrioles and maintaining centriole stability through the cell cycle.
claims.source: Together, these results indicate that compound microtubules are required for scaffolding substructures within centrioles and maintaining centriole stability through the cell cycle.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the collective data showing loss of inner scaffold and centriole disintegration in mutants.

claims.claim: About half of TEDC1-/- and TEDC2-/- mutant cells in asynchronous culture had no centrioles, and half had five or more centrioles.
claims.source: By immunofluorescence staining for two centriolar proteins, centrin (CETN) and CP110, we observed that TEDC1-/- and TEDC2-/- mutant cells had similar phenotypes to each other and to TUBD1-/- and TUBE1-/- mutant cells: in an asynchronously growing culture, about half of the cells had no centrioles, and half had five or more centrioles.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 1B showing centriole number distributions.

claims.claim: The phenotypes of TEDC1-/- and TEDC2-/- cells were fully rescued by expression of tagged TEDC1 or TEDC2.
claims.source: These phenotypes were fully rescued by expression of tagged TEDC1 (TEDC1-Halotag-3xFlag) or TEDC2 (TEDC2-V5-APEX2; Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 1 showing rescue of centriole phenotypes.

claims.claim: Almost all TEDC1-/- and TEDC2-/- mutant cells lacked centrioles in G0/G1 phase.
claims.source: We synchronized cells in each stage of the cell cycle, quantified the number of cells with centrioles, and found that almost all mutant cells lacked centrioles in G0/G1 phase.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 1B showing centriole numbers in synchronized cells.

claims.claim: Centrioles formed in S-phase in TEDC1-/- and TEDC2-/- mutant cells and disintegrated in M.
claims.source: Centrioles formed in S-phase and disintegrated in M (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 1B showing centriole numbers across cell cycle stages.

claims.claim: All centrioles in TEDC1-/- and TEDC2-/- mutant cells were positive for the procentriole marker SASS6.
claims.source: The centrioles that were present in mutant cells were immature: all centrioles were positive for the procentriole marker SASS6 and negative for the mature centriole marker CEP164 (Figure 1C and D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 1C showing SASS6 staining.

claims.claim: All centrioles in TEDC1-/- and TEDC2-/- mutant cells were negative for the mature centriole marker CEP164.
claims.source: The centrioles that were present in mutant cells were immature: all centrioles were positive for the procentriole marker SASS6 and negative for the mature centriole marker CEP164 (Figure 1C and D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 1D showing absence of CEP164 staining.

claims.claim: Centrioles in TEDC1-/- and TEDC2-/- mutant cells lacked compound microtubules and only had singlet microtubules.
claims.source: Similar to cells lacking delta-tubulin or epsilon-tubulin, we found that centrioles in TEDC1-/- and TEDC2-/- mutant cells lacked compound microtubules and only had singlet microtubules.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by TEM data in Figure 1E and F.

claims.claim: TEDC1-/- and TEDC2-/- mutant centrioles had cartwheels and pinheads.
claims.source: These centrioles had cartwheels and pinheads, but A-C linkers were not visible (Figure 1E and F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by TEM data in Figure 1E and F.

claims.claim: A-C linkers were not visible in TEDC1-/- and TEDC2-/- mutant centrioles.
claims.source: These centrioles had cartwheels and pinheads, but A-C linkers were not visible (Figure 1E and F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by TEM data in Figure 1E and F.

claims.claim: TEDC1 and TEDC2 are expressed at low levels in cells.
claims.source: TEDC1 and TEDC2 are expressed at low levels in cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and we could not reproducibly localize the endogenous proteins with antibody staining.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and F.

claims.claim: Tagged TEDC1 and TEDC2 rescue constructs localize to centrosomes.
claims.source: We found that the tagged rescue constructs localize to centrosomes (Figure 2A and B) and the antibodies for the tags were specific (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E-J).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2A and B.

claims.claim: TEDC1 and TEDC2 were enriched at centrosomes in S/G2 and colocalized with SASS6, but not centrin.
claims.source: TEDC1 and TEDC2 were enriched at centrosomes in S/G2 and colocalized with SASS6, but not centrin, indicating that TEDC1 and TEDC2 may localize to newly formed procentrioles and/or the proximal ends of parental centrioles.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2A and B showing colocalization patterns.

claims.claim: TEDC1 and TEDC2 may localize to newly formed procentrioles and/or the proximal ends of parental centrioles.
claims.source: TEDC1 and TEDC2 were enriched at centrosomes in S/G2 and colocalized with SASS6, but not centrin, indicating that TEDC1 and TEDC2 may localize to newly formed procentrioles and/or the proximal ends of parental centrioles.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the colocalization patterns observed in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Both TEDC1 and TEDC2 localize to procentrioles and the proximal ends of parental centrioles.
claims.source: With all three methods, we observed that both proteins localize to procentrioles and the proximal ends of parental centrioles.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple imaging methods shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: TEDC1 and TEDC2 overlap with the centriolar microtubules at procentrioles and proximal ends of parental centrioles.
claims.source: At these regions, both proteins overlap with the centriolar microtubules.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data in Figure 2C and D showing overlap with acetylated tubulin.

claims.claim: TEDC1 did not localize to centrioles in the absence of TEDC2, TUBD1, or TUBE1.
claims.source: We found that TEDC1 did not localize to centrioles in the absence of TEDC2, TUBD1, or TUBE1 (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: TEDC2 did not localize to centrioles in the absence of TEDC1, TUBD1, or TUBE1.
claims.source: Likewise, TEDC2 did not localize to centrioles in the absence of TEDC1, TUBD1, or TUBE1 (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Overexpression of TEDC1 or TEDC2 did not rescue the centriole phenotypes in any of the other mutants.
claims.source: Furthermore, overexpression of TEDC1 or TEDC2 did not rescue the centriole phenotypes in any of the other mutants, indicating that TEDC1 and TEDC2 are not downstream effectors of TUBD1 and TUBE1 (Figure 3A and B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 3A and B showing lack of rescue.

claims.claim: TEDC1 and TEDC2 are not downstream effectors of TUBD1 and TUBE1.
claims.source: Furthermore, overexpression of TEDC1 or TEDC2 did not rescue the centriole phenotypes in any of the other mutants, indicating that TEDC1 and TEDC2 are not downstream effectors of TUBD1 and TUBE1 (Figure 3A and B).
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the lack of rescue observed in Figure 3A and B.

claims.claim: TEDC1 did not interact with epsilon-tubulin in the absence of delta-tubulin.
claims.source: TEDC1 did not interact with epsilon-tubulin in the absence of delta-tubulin, nor did it interact with delta-tubulin in the absence of TUBE1.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by pulldown data in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: TEDC1 did not interact with delta-tubulin in the absence of TUBE1.
claims.source: TEDC1 did not interact with epsilon-tubulin in the absence of delta-tubulin, nor did it interact with delta-tubulin in the absence of TUBE1.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by pulldown data in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: In the absence of TEDC2, TEDC1 did not interact with TUBD1 or TUBE1.
claims.source: In the absence of TEDC2, TEDC1 did not interact with TUBD1 or TUBE1.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by pulldown data in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: In the absence of TUBD1 or TUBE1, TEDC1 and TEDC2 could still interact with each other.
claims.source: However, in the absence of TUBD1 or TUBE1, TEDC1 and TEDC2 could still interact with each other (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by pulldown data in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: TEDC2 did not interact with either tubulin in the absence of the other.
claims.source: TEDC2 did not interact with either tubulin in the absence of the other.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by pulldown data in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: In the absence of TEDC1, TEDC2 did not interact with either tubulin.
claims.source: In the absence of TEDC1, TEDC2 did not interact with either tubulin.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by pulldown data in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: AlphaFold-Multimer predicted that TUBD1 and TUBE1 would form a heterodimer, similar to the alpha-tubulin/beta-tubulin heterodimer, with TUBD1 at the minus-end of the heterodimer.
claims.source: AlphaFold-Multimer predicted that TUBD1 and TUBE1 would form a heterodimer, similar to the alpha-tubulin/beta-tubulin heterodimer, with TUBD1 at the minus-end of the heterodimer.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on computational prediction shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: AlphaFold predicted that the alpha-helices of TEDC1 and TEDC2 interact with each other.
claims.source: AlphaFold also predicted that the alpha-helices of TEDC1 and TEDC2 interact with each other, and that TEDC1 and TEDC2 form an interaction surface with TUBD1.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on computational prediction shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: AlphaFold predicted that TEDC1 and TEDC2 form an interaction surface with TUBD1.
claims.source: AlphaFold also predicted that the alpha-helices of TEDC1 and TEDC2 interact with each other, and that TEDC1 and TEDC2 form an interaction surface with TUBD1.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on computational prediction shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: The AlphaFold predictions at the interface between TEDC1, TEDC2, and TUBD1 yielded high confidence pLDDT and PAE scores.
claims.source: These predictions, especially at the interface between TEDC1, TEDC2, and TUBD1, yielded high confidence pLDDT and PAE scores (Figure 3E-G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the computational predictions shown in Figure 3E-G.

claims.claim: AlphaFold-Multimer did not predict a high-confidence interaction for TEDC1, TEDC2, alpha- and beta-tubulin.
claims.source: While AlphaFold-Multimer did not predict a high-confidence interaction for TEDC1, TEDC2, alpha- and beta-tubulin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), it did predict a high-confidence structure for Xenopus TEDC1, TEDC2, TUBD1, and TUBE1, similar to that predicted for the human proteins (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by computational predictions shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: AlphaFold-Multimer predicted a high-confidence structure for Xenopus TEDC1, TEDC2, TUBD1, and TUBE1, similar to that predicted for the human proteins.
claims.source: While AlphaFold-Multimer did not predict a high-confidence interaction for TEDC1, TEDC2, alpha- and beta-tubulin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), it did predict a high-confidence structure for Xenopus TEDC1, TEDC2, TUBD1, and TUBE1, similar to that predicted for the human proteins (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by computational predictions shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Antibodies against acetylated alpha-tubulin stained mutant centrioles well.
claims.source: We found that antibodies against acetylated alpha-tubulin stained mutant centrioles well (Figure 4B), indicating that centrioles with only singlet A-tubules can be acetylated.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Centrioles with only singlet A-tubules can be acetylated.
claims.source: We found that antibodies against acetylated alpha-tubulin stained mutant centrioles well (Figure 4B), indicating that centrioles with only singlet A-tubules can be acetylated.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the acetylated tubulin staining in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: In S-phase, centrioles were short in all conditions.
claims.source: In S-phase, centrioles were short in all conditions.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by length measurements in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: In G2-phase, centrioles elongated in all conditions, and mutant centrioles reached approximately similar lengths as control centrioles.
claims.source: In G2-phase, centrioles elongated in all conditions, and mutant centrioles reached approximately similar lengths as control centrioles (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by length measurements in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Mutant centriole widths did not increase and centrioles remained narrow.
claims.source: By contrast, mutant centriole widths did not increase and centrioles remained narrow, as we previously reported (Figure 4—figure supplement 5 and Wang et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by width measurements in Figure 4—figure supplement 5 and citation to prior work.

claims.claim: CEP120 was present and properly localized within mutant centrioles.
claims.source: Consistent with this hypothesis, CEP120, a protein involved in regulating centriole length (Comartin et al., 2013; Lin et al., 2013b; Mahjoub et al., 2010), was present and properly localized within mutant centrioles (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Mutant and control centrioles could be stained by GT335 antibody.
claims.source: We found that mutant and control centrioles could be stained by GT335 (Figure 4C), indicating that mutant centrioles are at least mono-glutamylated.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Mutant centrioles are at least mono-glutamylated.
claims.source: We found that mutant and control centrioles could be stained by GT335 (Figure 4C), indicating that mutant centrioles are at least mono-glutamylated.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on GT335 staining in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: The polyE antibody did not label control procentrioles or de novo centrioles in the first cell cycle after their formation.
claims.source: However, the polyE antibody did not label control procentrioles or de novo centrioles in the first cell cycle after their formation, making this antibody uninformative for our mutants (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Centriole glutamylation is a multi-step process, in which long glutamate side chains are added later during centriole maturation.
claims.source: These results show that centrioles with just singlet microtubules (A-tubules) can be mono-glutamylated. Moreover, similar to previous reports (Sullenberger et al., 2020), our results suggest that centriole glutamylation is a multi-step process, in which long glutamate side chains are added later during centriole maturation.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the differential staining with GT335 and polyE antibodies, supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: TEDC1-/- and TEDC2-/- mutant centrioles failed to recruit POC5.
claims.source: Using expansion microscopy, we found that TEDC1-/- and TEDC2-/- mutant centrioles also failed to recruit POC5 (Figure 4Ei).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data in Figure 4Ei.

claims.claim: The helical inner scaffold is not properly formed in centrioles with singlet microtubules.
claims.source: Since our original work was published, POC5 was shown to be a component of the helical inner scaffold within the central core. These results indicate that the helical inner scaffold is not properly formed in centrioles with singlet microtubules.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the absence of POC5 in mutant centrioles shown in Figure 4Ei.

claims.claim: WDR90 was not recruited to mutant centrioles.
claims.source: We found that WDR90 was not recruited to mutant centrioles, in contrast to control centrioles, in which it is recruited in G2-phase (Figure 4Eii).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data in Figure 4Eii.

claims.claim: Mutant centrioles with singlet microtubules fail to build or stabilize the inner junction between the A- and B-tubules.
claims.source: From these results, it is likely that mutant centrioles with singlet microtubules fail to build or stabilize the inner junction between the A- and B-tubules.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the absence of WDR90 in mutant centrioles.

claims.claim: In the absence of the inner junction and junctional protein WDR90, centrioles with singlet microtubules cannot form the inner scaffold.
claims.source: In the absence of the inner junction and junctional protein WDR90, centrioles with singlet microtubules cannot form the inner scaffold.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the absence of both WDR90 and POC5 in mutant centrioles.

claims.claim: Gamma-tubulin was not detected within the lumen of control or de novo-formed centrioles in S or G2-phase.
claims.source: As also previously reported (Laporte et al., 2024), we failed to detect gamma-tubulin within the lumen of control or de novo-formed centrioles in S or G2-phase (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E) and thus were unable to test whether gamma-tubulin, which is recruited to the lumen of centrioles by the inner scaffold, was mislocalized in mutant centrioles.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E and citation to prior work.

claims.claim: SASS6 was present within the lumen of control and mutant centrioles in S-phase.
claims.source: We found that the centriolar cartwheel protein, SASS6, was present within the lumen of control and mutant centrioles in S-phase.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: In control centrioles in G2-phase, SASS6 was restricted to just the proximal end.
claims.source: In control centrioles in G2-phase, SASS6 was restricted to just the proximal end.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: SASS6 was elongated in all G2-phase mutant centrioles.
claims.source: Surprisingly, SASS6 was elongated in all G2-phase mutant centrioles (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 4F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: CEP135, STIL, CPAP, and CEP44 showed elongated localization in mutant centrioles similar to SASS6.
claims.source: We observed a similar phenotype with multiple other proximal-end proteins: CEP135, STIL, CPAP, and CEP44 (Figure 4G-I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 3), indicating that the entire proximal end is elongated in mutant centrioles.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data in Figure 4G-I and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: The entire proximal end is elongated in mutant centrioles.
claims.source: We observed a similar phenotype with multiple other proximal-end proteins: CEP135, STIL, CPAP, and CEP44 (Figure 4G-I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 3), indicating that the entire proximal end is elongated in mutant centrioles.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the elongated localization of multiple proximal end proteins.

claims.claim: The extended localization of proximal end proteins was not due to increased protein expression in mutant cells.
claims.source: The extended localization of proximal end proteins was not due to increased protein expression in mutant cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: CETN2 and CP110 were localized to mutant centrioles and clearly marked one end of the centriole barrel in both S-phase and G2-phase.
claims.source: We found that CETN2 and CP110, two proteins of the distal centriole, were localized to mutant centrioles and clearly marked one end of the centriole barrel in both S-phase and G2-phase (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C.

claims.claim: Proximal-to-distal centriole polarity was unaffected in mutant centrioles.
claims.source: We conclude that proximal-to-distal centriole polarity was unaffected in mutant centrioles, and proximal end elongation did not affect the recruitment of proteins to the centriole distal end.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the proper localization of distal end proteins in mutant centrioles.

claims.claim: Proximal end elongation did not affect the recruitment of proteins to the centriole distal end.
claims.source: We conclude that proximal-to-distal centriole polarity was unaffected in mutant centrioles, and proximal end elongation did not affect the recruitment of proteins to the centriole distal end.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the proper localization of distal end proteins despite proximal end elongation.

claims.claim: Centrioles lacking compound microtubules are unable to properly regulate the length of the proximal end.
claims.source: Together, these results indicate that centrioles lacking compound microtubules are unable to properly regulate the length of the proximal end.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the elongated proximal end observed in mutant centrioles.

claims.claim: CEP295 was present and normally localized within mutant centrioles in both S- and G2-phases.
claims.source: Using U-ExM, we found that CEP295 was present and normally localized within mutant centrioles in both S- and G2-phases (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claims.claim: Centriole loss in mutants is unlikely to be due to loss of CEP295 localization.
claims.source: We conclude that centriole loss in our mutants is unlikely to be due to loss of CEP295 localization, and therefore that TEDC1, TEDC2, TUBD1, and TUBE1 are likely part of a different pathway required for centriole stability through the cell cycle.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the normal CEP295 localization in mutant centrioles.

claims.claim: TEDC1, TEDC2, TUBD1, and TUBE1 are likely part of a different pathway required for centriole stability through the cell cycle.
claims.source: We conclude that centriole loss in our mutants is unlikely to be due to loss of CEP295 localization, and therefore that TEDC1, TEDC2, TUBD1, and TUBE1 are likely part of a different pathway required for centriole stability through the cell cycle.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the normal CEP295 localization despite centriole loss.

claims.claim: In prometaphase stage TUBD1-/- or TUBE1-/- cells, centrioles were longer than normal, with an elongated proximal end marked by SASS6, and a CP110-positive cap.
claims.source: By contrast, in prometaphase stage TUBD1-/- or TUBE1-/- cells, we found that centrioles had a unique appearance: they were longer than normal, with an elongated proximal end marked by SASS6, and a CP110-positive cap.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data in Figure 5C and E.

claims.claim: The two ends of prometaphase mutant centrioles were connected by weak monoE staining.
claims.source: These two ends were connected by weak monoE staining (Figure 5C and E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data in Figure 5C and E.

claims.claim: After metaphase, centrioles in mutant cells were either completely absent, or had a fragmented appearance.
claims.source: After metaphase, centrioles in mutant cells were either completely absent, or had a fragmented appearance (Figure 5D and F), with aggregates of staining that did not resemble true centrioles.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data in Figure 5D and F.

claims.claim: In mutant cells, centrioles elongate in early mitosis to form an aberrant intermediate structure, followed by fragmentation in late mitosis.
claims.source: We conclude that in our mutant cells, centrioles elongate in early mitosis to form an aberrant intermediate structure, followed by fragmentation in late mitosis.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the progression of centriole changes observed in Figure 5.

claims.claim: The absence of the inner scaffold arises from the loss of the B- and C-tubules within centrioles.
claims.source: We propose that the absence of the inner scaffold arises from the loss of the B- and C-tubules within centrioles, which may serve to anchor WDR90 and/or other proteins of the inner scaffold.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data showing absence of inner scaffold in mutant centrioles.

claims.claim: The B- and C-tubules may serve to anchor WDR90 and/or other proteins of the inner scaffold.
claims.source: We propose that the absence of the inner scaffold arises from the loss of the B- and C-tubules within centrioles, which may serve to anchor WDR90 and/or other proteins of the inner scaffold.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data.

claims.claim: WDR90 has been proposed to localize to the inner junction between the A- and B-tubules and is required for recruiting other inner scaffold components.
claims.source: WDR90 has been proposed to localize to the inner junction between the A- and B-tubules and is required for recruiting other inner scaffold components (Le Guennec et al., 2020; Steib et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: The B-tubule is required to recruit or stabilize WDR90 at the inner junction.
claims.source: We find that mutant centrioles with singlet microtubules fail to localize WDR90, and thus speculate that the B-tubule is required to recruit or stabilize WDR90 at the inner junction.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the absence of WDR90 in mutant centrioles lacking B-tubules.

claims.claim: The inner scaffold makes connections to all three (A-, B-, and C-) tubules by cryo-electron tomography.

results.result: Loss of TEDC1 or TEDC2 phenocopies loss of delta-tubulin or epsilon-tubulin. TEDC1-/- and TEDC2-/- cells exhibit a futile cycle of centriole formation and disintegration, with centrioles forming in S-phase and disintegrating in M-phase. These mutant centrioles lack compound microtubules, contain only singlet microtubules, and remain immature (SASS6-positive, CEP164-negative).
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C37-C51 collectively demonstrate that TEDC1-/- and TEDC2-/- mutants phenocopy TUBD1-/- and TUBE1-/- mutants through multiple lines of evidence: immunofluorescence showing centriole number distributions across cell cycle stages (C43, C45, C46), maturation markers (C47, C48), TEM showing singlet microtubules (C49), and presence of cartwheels/pinheads but absence of A-C linkers (C50, C51). The phenotypes are fully rescued by tagged constructs (C44), confirming specificity.

results.result: TEDC1 and TEDC2 localize to centrosomes, specifically to procentrioles and the proximal ends of parental centrioles. Both proteins are enriched at centrosomes in S/G2 phase, colocalize with SASS6 but not centrin, and overlap with centriolar microtubules at these regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C53-C57 are well-supported by multiple imaging approaches including immunofluorescence (Figure 2A, B), super-resolution microscopy (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B), and U-ExM (Figure 2C, D). The colocalization patterns with SASS6 but not centrin (C54) provide strong evidence for the specific localization to procentrioles and proximal ends of parental centrioles (C55, C56).

results.result: TEDC1 and TEDC2 are mutually dependent on each other and on delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin for centrosomal localization. TEDC1 and TEDC2 are not downstream effectors of TUBD1 and TUBE1, as overexpression does not rescue centriole phenotypes in other mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C58-C61 are supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3A and 3B showing loss of TEDC1 or TEDC2 centrosomal localization in various mutant backgrounds. The lack of rescue by overexpression (C60) provides strong evidence that these proteins function together in a complex rather than in a linear pathway (C61).

results.result: TEDC1, TEDC2, TUBD1, and TUBE1 physically interact in a complex. TEDC1 and TEDC2 can form a subcomplex in the absence of the tubulins, but interactions with the tubulins require all four proteins to be present.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C8, C62-C67 are supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments in Figure 3C and 3D. The data show that TEDC1-TEDC2 can interact independently of tubulins (C8, C65), but TEDC1 or TEDC2 cannot interact with either tubulin in the absence of the other tubulin or the other TEDC protein (C62-C64, C66, C67). This demonstrates a tetrameric complex with specific interaction requirements.

results.result: AlphaFold-Multimer predicts a high-confidence tetrameric structure for TEDC1, TEDC2, TUBD1, and TUBE1. The model predicts TUBD1 and TUBE1 form a heterodimer similar to alpha/beta-tubulin, with TEDC1 and TEDC2 alpha-helices interacting with each other and forming an interaction surface with TUBD1.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C71, C73 are supported by computational predictions shown in Figure 3E-G with high confidence pLDDT and PAE scores at the TEDC1-TEDC2-TUBD1 interface. The prediction is consistent across species (Xenopus, C73) and with experimental pulldown data showing TEDC1-TEDC2 can form a subcomplex. However, these are computational predictions that require experimental validation of the predicted structure.

results.result: Mutant centrioles elongate to approximately the same length as control centrioles in G2 phase but remain narrow. In S-phase, centrioles are short in all conditions, but in G2-phase, mutant centrioles reach similar lengths to controls while maintaining reduced width.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C76-C78 are supported by U-ExM length measurements in Figure 4A showing statistically significant elongation from S to G2 phase in all conditions (p<0.0001), with mutant centrioles reaching similar lengths to controls. Width measurements in Figure 4—figure supplement 5 confirm mutant centrioles remain narrow (C78), consistent with prior work (Wang et al., 2017).

results.result: Mutant centrioles fail to recruit central core scaffold proteins POC5 and WDR90, indicating that compound microtubules are required for proper formation of the helical inner scaffold. Mutant centrioles with singlet microtubules likely fail to build or stabilize the inner junction between A- and B-tubules.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C39, C84-C88, C113 are supported by U-ExM data in Figure 4Ei and 4Eii showing absence of POC5 and WDR90 in mutant centrioles. The inference that compound microtubules are required for inner scaffold formation (C85, C113) is well-supported by the data. The proposed mechanism involving failure to build the inner junction (C87, C88) is a reasonable inference based on WDR90's known role at the A-B junction.

results.result: Mutant centrioles have an expanded proximal region with elongated localization of multiple proximal end proteins (SASS6, CEP135, STIL, CPAP, CEP44). In control centrioles, these proteins are restricted to the proximal end in G2-phase, but in mutant centrioles they extend throughout the entire centriole length.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C40, C90-C94, C99 are supported by U-ExM data in Figure 4F-I and supplementary figures showing elongated localization of multiple proximal end proteins in G2-phase mutant centrioles. The phenotype is consistent across multiple proteins (C93) and is not due to increased protein expression (C95, Figure 4—figure supplement 2). This represents a novel architectural defect in mutant centrioles.

results.result: During mitosis, mutant centrioles undergo a stereotyped progression of changes: elongation in prometaphase with an elongated proximal end and CP110-positive cap connected by weak monoE staining, followed by fragmentation and complete loss in late mitosis. Centriole loss is correlated with loss of the SASS6 cartwheel.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C103-C106, C126 are supported by U-ExM data in Figure 5 showing the progression of centriole changes through mitosis. The prometaphase elongation (C103, C104) and subsequent fragmentation (C105) are clearly documented. The correlation with SASS6 loss (C126) provides insight into the mechanism of centriole disintegration.

results.result: Centrioles formed de novo are very similar to procentrioles formed by templated centriole duplication in composition and architecture.
results.evaluation: Claim C41 is supported by comparative U-ExM data throughout Figure 4 showing similar protein localization patterns between de novo centrioles and control procentrioles for multiple markers including acetylated tubulin, glutamylation, POC5, WDR90, and proximal end proteins. This addresses a gap in knowledge about de novo centriole architecture.

results.result: Mutant centrioles with only singlet A-tubules can be acetylated and mono-glutamylated. GT335 antibody stains both control and mutant centrioles, but polyE antibody does not label control procentrioles or de novo centrioles in the first cell cycle, suggesting glutamylation is a multi-step process.
results.evaluation: Claims C74, C75, C80-C83 are supported by U-ExM data in Figure 4B and 4C showing acetylated tubulin and GT335 staining of mutant centrioles. The inference that A-tubules alone can be acetylated and mono-glutamylated (C75, C81) is well-supported. The multi-step glutamylation model (C83) is consistent with prior work (Sullenberger et al., 2020) and the differential staining patterns.

results.result: Many aspects of centriole architecture are unaffected in mutant centrioles, including distal tip formation, centriole length regulation prior to mitosis, acquisition of post-translational modifications, and establishment of proximal-distal polarity. Proteins regulating these processes can act on the A-tubule independently of B- and C-tubules.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C98, C121-C122 are supported by U-ExM data throughout Figure 4 showing normal localization of distal end proteins (CETN2, CP110), CEP120, CEP295, and maintenance of proximal-distal polarity in mutant centrioles. This demonstrates that many centriole assembly processes are independent of compound microtubule formation.

results.result: CEP295 is properly localized in mutant centrioles in both S- and G2-phases, indicating that centriole loss in mutants is unlikely due to loss of CEP295 localization and may be independent of centriole-to-centrosome conversion. TEDC1, TEDC2, TUBD1, and TUBE1 are likely part of a different pathway required for centriole stability.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C102, C125 are supported by U-ExM data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F showing normal CEP295 localization in mutant centrioles. The inference that centriole loss occurs through a different mechanism than CEP295-dependent centriole-to-centrosome conversion (C101, C102, C125) is reasonable given the data, though the exact mechanism remains to be determined.

results.result: The authors propose that the absence of the inner scaffold arises from loss of B- and C-tubules, which may serve to anchor WDR90 and/or other inner scaffold proteins. The B-tubule may be required to recruit or stabilize WDR90 at the inner junction.
results.evaluation: Claims C107, C108, C110 are explicitly stated as speculation ('we propose', 'may serve', 'speculate') based on the absence of WDR90 in mutant centrioles. While the model is consistent with the data and WDR90's known role at the A-B junction (C109), these are mechanistic hypotheses that require direct experimental testing to be considered supported.

results.result: The authors speculate that triplet microtubules, the inner scaffold, and/or the TUBD1/TUBE1/TEDC1/TEDC2 complex might act to limit the length of the proximal end. The height of the cartwheel may be regulated by triplet microtubules through interdependent assembly with centriolar microtubules.
results.evaluation: Claims C114, C118, C120 are explicitly stated as speculation ('it is possible', 'may be regulated') about mechanisms regulating proximal end length. While the elongated proximal end phenotype is well-documented, these mechanistic hypotheses require additional experiments to test. The comparison with POC1A-/- centrioles (C117) provides some support but is insufficient to confirm the proposed mechanisms.

results.result: The authors speculate about possible structural roles for the TEDC1/TEDC2/TUBD1/TUBE1 complex, including formation of A-C linkers, pinheads, or triplet base. It is unclear whether loss of A-C linkers is due to direct or indirect roles of these proteins. The complex may interact transiently with centrioles or only some proteins may form structural components.
results.evaluation: Claims C145-C149 are explicitly stated as speculation ('it is possible', 'it is not clear', 'we note') about the structural role of the complex. While DepMap co-dependencies with A-C linker components (C146) provide some support, the authors acknowledge uncertainty about direct vs. indirect roles (C147) and alternative models (C148, C149). These hypotheses require additional structural and functional studies.

results.result: TEDC1-/- and TEDC2-/- cells phenocopy the loss of TUBD1 or TUBE1, showing similar centriole abnormalities including a futile cycle of centriole formation in S-phase and disintegration in mitosis, with mutant centrioles lacking compound microtubules and having only singlet microtubules.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirm this core finding. Reviewer 1 states 'the authors show that all four proteins function as a complex and knockout of any of the four proteins results in the same phenotype.' Reviewer 2 notes 'The results are very convincing, particularly the phenotype, which is the same as previously observed for TUBD1 and TUBE1.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'the authors show that human cells lacking the associated proteins TEDC1 or TEDC2 have these identical phenotypes.' The editor summarizes this as a key finding supported by 'convincing evidence based on knockout cell lines.'

results.result: TEDC1, TEDC2, TUBD1, and TUBE1 physically interact to form a complex, with TEDC1 and TEDC2 able to form a subcomplex in the absence of the tubulins, and all four proteins being mutually dependent for their centrosomal localization.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm the biochemical interaction data. Reviewer 2 states 'The authors also report convincing results on direct interactions between TUBD1, TUBE1, TEDC1, and TEDC2.' Reviewer 1 notes the study shows 'all four proteins function as a complex.' The editor confirms the work is 'supported by convincing evidence based on...immunoprecipitation.' No reviewer raises concerns about the interaction or dependency data.

results.result: TEDC1 and TEDC2 localize to centrosomes, specifically to procentrioles and the proximal ends of parental centrioles, where they overlap with centriolar microtubules and colocalize with SASS6 but not centrin.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm the localization findings despite acknowledging technical challenges. Reviewer 2 states 'The U-ExM localization is also convincing: despite a signal that's not very homogeneous, it's clear that the complex is in the proximal region of the centriole and procentriole.' Reviewer 3 notes 'it is evident that these proteins occupy growing centrioles and the proximal parts of mother centrioles.' Reviewer 1 acknowledges 'The precise mapping of TED complex proteins to centrioles remains challenging with the available tools but has been addressed through the use of several complementary super-resolution techniques.'

results.result: AlphaFold-Multimer predicts that TUBD1 and TUBE1 form a heterodimer similar to alpha/beta-tubulin, with TEDC1 and TEDC2 forming interacting alpha-helices that create an interaction surface with TUBD1, yielding high confidence scores at the interface.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly affirms this finding, stating the authors present 'an intriguing structural prediction suggesting that TEDC1 and TEDC2 form a heterodimer that interacts with the TUBD1-TUBE1 heterodimer.' No reviewer challenges the computational predictions or their interpretation. The high confidence scores and consistency across species (human and Xenopus) are presented without critique.

results.result: Mutant centrioles elongate to approximately the same length as control centrioles in G2 phase, but remain narrow in width, indicating that length regulation is preserved while width expansion is impaired.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding without challenge. Reviewer 1 notes the study uses 'detailed quantifications' and presents data that is 'well-performed' and 'convincing.' The length and width measurements are part of the comprehensive U-ExM characterization that all reviewers affirm as convincing evidence.

results.result: Mutant centrioles fail to recruit central core scaffold proteins including POC5 and WDR90, indicating that compound microtubules are required for proper formation of the inner helical scaffold and that centrioles with singlet microtubules cannot form the inner scaffold.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this finding. Reviewer 1 states 'They further find that mutant centrioles lack inner scaffold proteins...suggesting that triplet microtubule formation is linked to...formation of the central region that contains the inner scaffold.' results.result: Mutant centrioles have an expanded proximal region with elongated localization of SASS6, CEP135, STIL, CPAP, and CEP44, indicating that compound microtubules are required for correctly positioning and limiting the length of the proximal end.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this striking finding. Reviewer 2 states 'The phenotype observed in U-ExM on the elongation of the cartwheel is also spectacular and opens the question of the regulation of the size of this structure.' Reviewer 1 notes mutant centrioles 'contain an extended proximal end including markers such as SAS6 and CEP135.' No reviewer challenges this observation or its interpretation.

results.result: During mitosis, mutant centrioles further elongate in prometaphase before fragmenting and disintegrating in later mitotic stages, with centriole loss correlated with loss of the SASS6 cartwheel.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding with a minor caveat. Reviewer 1 notes 'they show that mutant centrioles seem to undergo elongation during early mitosis before disassembly, although it is not clear if this may also be due to prolonged mitotic duration in mutants.' This uncertainty about mechanism does not challenge the observation itself, which is supported by the U-ExM data that reviewers find convincing.

results.result: Centrioles formed de novo are very similar to procentrioles formed by templated centriole duplication in composition and architecture.
results.evaluation: This finding is implicitly supported through the reviewers' acceptance of the comparative data throughout Figure 4. No reviewer challenges the comparison between de novo and templated centrioles, and the comprehensive characterization using U-ExM is affirmed as convincing by all reviewers.

results.result: Mutant centrioles with only singlet A-tubules can be acetylated and mono-glutamylated, indicating that these post-translational modifications do not require compound microtubules, though long glutamate side chains are added later during maturation.
results.evaluation: This finding is part of the comprehensive characterization that reviewers affirm. Reviewer 1 notes the study shows 'Many aspects of centriole architecture...including...acquisition of post-translational modifications, are unaffected in mutant centrioles.' The data on glutamylation is presented without challenge from any reviewer.

results.result: Many aspects of centriole architecture are unaffected in mutant centrioles, including formation of the distal tip, proximal-distal polarity, and recruitment of proteins like CETN2, CP110, and CEP295, indicating these processes can act on the A-tubule independently of B- and C-tubules.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this comprehensive characterization. Reviewer 1 states the study is 'well-performed' with 'conclusions supported by convincing data' and 'detailed quantifications.' The preservation of many centriole features despite loss of compound microtubules is part of the overall phenotypic characterization that all reviewers find convincing.
